outcome: Describe eukaryotic cells as having a nucleus, and bacterial cells as smaller with a cell wall, a free DNA loop and plasmids.
Compare the size and scale of cells using order-of-magnitude estimates, standard form and metric prefixes.
Explain how the nucleus, membrane, mitochondria, ribosomes, chloroplasts, vacuole, cell wall and plasmids relate to their functions.
List the parts of a typical animal cell and the extra parts found in plant and algal cells.
Use a light microscope to observe, draw and label cells with a magnification scale (required practical 1).
Explain how the structure of a specialised cell suits its function in a tissue, organ or whole organism.
Give examples of specialised cells: sperm, nerve and muscle in animals; root hair, xylem and phloem in plants.
Explain why cell differentiation matters as an organism develops.
Contrast animal cells, which mostly differentiate early, with plant cells that can differentiate throughout life.
State that in mature animals cell division mainly serves repair and replacement, and that differentiation gives a cell its specialised structures.
Explain how the development of microscopy, especially electron microscopy, improved understanding of sub-cellular structures.
Compare light and electron microscopes in magnification and resolving power.
Calculate magnification, real size and image size, using prefixes and standard form.
State that bacteria divide by binary fission as often as every 20 minutes given nutrients and warmth.
Describe growing bacteria in nutrient broth or as colonies on agar plates.
Describe aseptic technique for an uncontaminated culture and explain the sterilising, taping and 25 degree incubation steps.
Calculate bacterial population after a time from the mean division time, and the area of colonies or clear zones using pi r squared.
Investigate the effect of antiseptics or antibiotics on bacterial growth using zones of inhibition (required practical 2).
State that the nucleus holds chromosomes made of DNA, each carrying many genes, usually in pairs in body cells.
Describe the cell cycle: growth, DNA replication, then mitosis and division of cytoplasm and membranes into two identical cells.
Explain why mitosis matters for growth and development and recognise it in given situations.
Define a stem cell and describe its role in embryos, adult bone marrow and plant meristems.
Describe how stem cells and therapeutic cloning may treat conditions such as diabetes and paralysis, and why the body will not reject them.
Evaluate risks and ethical or religious objections to stem cell use.
Explain how plant meristem cells can be cloned to protect rare species or produce disease-resistant crops.
Define diffusion and give examples such as oxygen, carbon dioxide and urea moving across membranes.
Explain how concentration gradient, temperature and surface area affect the rate of diffusion.
Explain why single-celled organisms exchange enough without special systems, and calculate and compare surface area to volume ratios.
Explain why multicellular organisms need exchange surfaces and a transport system.
Explain how the small intestine, lungs, gills, roots and leaves are adapted for exchange.
State that exchange surfaces work better with large area, thin membrane, good blood supply and ventilation.
Define osmosis as the diffusion of water across a partially permeable membrane from dilute to concentrated solution.
Calculate rate of water uptake and percentage mass change of plant tissue, and plot and interpret graphs.
Investigate how salt or sugar concentration changes plant tissue mass (required practical 3).
Describe active transport as movement against a concentration gradient that needs energy from respiration.
Give examples: mineral ions into root hairs and sugar from the gut into the blood.
Explain the differences between diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
